title: Linear Equations — Chapter Summary
intro: An equation says two algebraic expressions are equal; solving it means finding the values that make the two sides match. When the variable appears only to the first power, the equation is linear. This chapter develops the techniques to solve linear equations in one variable, then in two variables (where two equations are needed), and the word problems that translate real situations into algebra.

sections.heading: Linear Equation in One Variable
bullets: Standard form: ax + b = 0 with a ≠ 0.
The unique solution is x = −b/a.
Equality properties: add / subtract / multiply / divide both sides by the same NON-ZERO number.
Verify by substituting the candidate solution into the ORIGINAL equation.

sections.heading: Solving Linear Equations — Strategy
bullets: Step 1: Clear denominators by multiplying both sides by the LCM.
Step 2: Remove brackets using the distributive law.
Step 3: Bring all variable terms to one side, all constants to the other.
Step 4: Combine like terms and divide by the coefficient of x.
Step 5: Verify by substitution.
If all variable terms cancel and the result is a true statement (e.g. 3 = 3), the original equation is an identity. If the result is false (e.g. 3 = 5), the equation has NO solution.

sections.heading: Word Problems — One Variable
bullets: Routine: read carefully, name x, translate, form ONE equation, solve, verify, translate back.
Number puzzles: consecutive integers x, x + 1, x + 2; consecutive odd / even x, x + 2, x + 4.
Age problems: write 'present age' first; build the future / past expressions.
Geometry: perimeter / area constraints.
Money / ratio: link rates and totals.
Recognise non-linear translations early — some problems lead to a quadratic and need Chapter 6.

sections.heading: Linear Equations in Two Variables
bullets: Standard form: ax + by + c = 0 with a, b not both zero.
A solution is an ORDERED PAIR (x, y) satisfying the equation.
Every linear equation in two variables has INFINITELY MANY solutions.
Geometrically, the solution set is a STRAIGHT LINE in the xy-plane.
Graphing: pick two convenient x's, compute y, plot, draw the line; a third point is a check.

sections.heading: Systems of Two Linear Equations
bullets: Two equations are needed to pin down (x, y) uniquely.
Three cases:
• Unique solution — a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂ (lines intersect once).
• No solution — a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂ (parallel lines).
• Infinitely many — a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂ (same line).
Apply the ratio test before solving — it tells you which case you're in.
Methods: substitution, elimination (addition / subtraction), cross-multiplication.
Pick the method that fits the coefficients.

sections.heading: Word Problems — Two Variables
bullets: Two unknowns ⇒ name x and y; translate two distinct facts into two equations.
Money / quantity: 'a pencils + b erasers = ₹X' style.
Speed in a current: still-water speed x, current y; downstream = x + y, upstream = x − y.
Two-rate investment / mixture problems.
If the natural translation is non-linear, consider a substitution u = 1/(x − y) etc. that turns the system linear.

key_takeaways: Linear means first-degree — variables to the first power, no products of variables, no division by a variable.
ax + b = 0 has the unique solution x = −b/a.
Strategy for solving: clear denominators, distribute, isolate, divide, verify.
A linear equation in two variables has infinitely many solutions — a line in the xy-plane.
Two equations are needed to pin down a unique pair (x, y).
Apply the ratio test on coefficients to classify a 2×2 system in advance.
Choose the solution method that fits: substitution if a coefficient is 1; elimination otherwise; cross-multiplication for awkward systems.
For word problems: translate, solve, verify — and recognise non-linear translations early.

glossary.definition: A statement that two algebraic expressions are equal.
An equation in which every variable appears only to the first power, with no products of variables and no division by any variable.
A value (or ordered tuple of values) that makes the two sides of the equation equal.
A rule for transforming an equation while preserving its solution set: add, subtract, multiply or divide both sides by the same non-zero number.
An equation of the form ax + by + c = 0 with (a, b) ≠ (0, 0).
A pair (x₀, y₀) that satisfies the linear equation in two variables when substituted.
A set of two (or more) linear equations in the same variables, considered together.
A system that has at least one solution.
A system that has no solution.
Solve one equation for one variable, substitute into the other, solve the resulting one-variable equation.
Multiply equations by suitable constants so one variable's coefficients match (in magnitude); add or subtract to eliminate that variable.
A formula-based method that returns x and y as ratios of certain coefficient combinations of the two equations.
